And then everybody from the vision community have, have been, switching to vision transformers from more traditional convnets, and they are getting better and better performance. So in, so in this work, we want to say, we want to investigate, whether truly, like, convnet is, has lost its, competitiveness, and whether it's possible to, to, control all the design components there is to study whether convnets can be modernized to be, on par with vision transformers at that time.

So we wanna study whether it's a, it's a difference that seeming, seemingly, performance gap between transform- vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution or due to other small, like seemingly small design details. So, and we found the answer to be, the latter. So after a lot of studying, in, of like modernizing the design compon- components of a convnet, we eventually get the model to be on par with, vision transformers, very strong vision transformers at that time on a diverse range of tasks. So this demonstrates that, no matter you choose convnet or vision transformers, as long as you get the des- the, everything correct, you'll, you'll get, the same frontier level performance on vision tasks.

Yeah.

Zhuang Liu: I wouldn't s-- Yeah, I, I largely tend to agree, but I wou- I wouldn't say it doesn't matter. it's, I, I would say, as long as you get everything correct, like as long as you have, y- explore the s- the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's like kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. like I think in the past, many years, there haven't been real- really, like innovations that, have been widely adopted other than the, kind of the mature architectures that we, we already were working with, several years ago. but, but this process itself is very, very fun. in fact, recently there have been some, paper releases on this, especially from this, open, open weight model companies like Kimi, DeepSeek.

And how, how do we measure this? We, we designed a very dumb experiment that's, doesn't make sense at all as a, as a, like, a deep learning training, program. What we did is this. given three very large scale computer vision datasets, we train and classify neural network to classify, to classify which, which dataset a given particular image comes from. It's not a practical problem, it's just to try to guess the dataset's origin. it's a multi-ca- multiclass classification problem. It turns out, even with these seemingly non-- very diverse datasets, the model can still tell this answer with surprisingly high accuracy, up to, more, higher than 80% accuracy when, when you have three datasets.

Mm-hmm. Right. So MMVP stands for Multimodal Visual Patterns. And the motivation was really to understand, when a multimodal model gets a very simple visual question wrong, where does that failure come from? Is it that the language model cannot reason about the image, or that it hasn't actually received the information it needs?

So we looked at what we call CLIP-blind pairs. These are pairs of images that have very similar representations according to CLIP, but, to a human, there are clear visual differences. And we can ask questions about those differences that are very easy for people to answer. You don't need complicated reasoning. You just need to look at the image, right? But if the vision encoder represents those two images almost the same way, then the downstream language model has a very difficult job distinguishing them.

And that's the connection to what I was saying earlier. We give the language model these vision tokens, and then we expect it to answer everything about the image. But if some important detail wasn't preserved in those tokens, making the language model stronger doesn't necessarily solve that problem. It might make a better guess from its language knowledge, but that is different from actually seeing the detail.

So, for these kinds of failures, I think the vision encoder is a very important bottleneck. But I wouldn't say every multimodal failure is a vision problem. Even when the information is there, you still need the alignment and the language model to use it correctly. These are connected problems.

The lesson for me is that we shouldn't assume perception is already solved just because we have a strong vision encoder. A representation can be very good at matching an image with a general description, while still missing details that matter for answering a specific question. And MMVP is trying to make that gap visible. Yeah.

sol.text:
Yeah. So MMVP stands for the Multimodal Visual Patterns benchmark. The basic idea is very simple: we first identify what we call CLIP-blind pairs—pairs of images that are clearly different to a human, often in a way that changes the answer to a question, but that a CLIP-like vision encoder maps to very similar representations. Then we ask multimodal language models questions that require noticing exactly that difference.

What we found is that many models fail consistently on these pairs. And the important point is that the language model may already have the knowledge and reasoning ability needed to answer the question. But if the vision encoder has compressed away the relevant distinction—say, a spatial relation, an orientation, a count, or whether some detail is present—the language model never receives that information. Once it is lost at the encoder, a better prompt or a stronger language model cannot reliably reconstruct it.

So I would say a substantial part of this bottleneck is genuinely a vision problem. It comes from the objective and data used to train CLIP-like encoders: they are very good at semantic alignment, at recognizing that two images are broadly about the same thing, but that can encourage invariance to fine-grained details that are actually essential for visual question answering. Of course, it is not purely a vision problem. The connector, the multimodal alignment training, and the language model’s use of visual tokens also matter. But the CLIP-blind-pair experiment gives us a useful diagnosis: if the relevant distinction is already absent from the visual representation, the downstream components have very little chance.

And I think the broader lesson is that better multimodal models cannot come only from attaching a more capable LLM to the same frozen vision encoder. We also need vision representations that preserve fine-grained, spatial, and task-relevant information, perhaps through better visual pretraining, higher-resolution or local features, multiple complementary encoders, or more end-to-end training. Yeah.

r001.rationale: The response discusses CLIP-like encoders favoring broad semantic alignment and losing spatial information, but does not clearly identify image-caption training or explicitly explain the lack of object-position learning.

r002.rationale: It recommends better visual pretraining and task-relevant representations, but does not state that models must be trained on spatial-relational tasks or objectives.

opus.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, so, so MMVP stands for Multimodal Visual Patterns. it's a benchmark we, we built in that paper. so let me, let me first describe how, how the whole thing started, because the, the construction is, is kind of the, the core idea of the paper.

So, back then, everybody was, was very excited about, GPT-4V and, and all these multimodal LLMs, and, and they seem to be able to do everything. but at the same time, if you, if you play with them a little bit, you, you would notice they fail on some really, really simple questions. Like, questions that any, any human, like a, a child could answer immediately. So the, the question is, is this random, or is there some, some systematic, structure to these failures?

So, so what we did is, we, we used CLIP and DINOv2 together. we look for, pairs of images that CLIP thinks are almost identical, like very high similarity in the CLIP embedding space, but DINOv2, which is a, a vision-only self-supervised model, says they are, they are clearly different. And we call these CLIP-blind pairs. and then we, we look at these pairs by hand and ask, okay, what is actually different between these two images? Is the, is the dog facing left or right, how many, how many wheels are there, is the, is the door open or closed. and, and we turn that into a very simple visual question. and, and it turns out that, these, these models, they, they, they fail, like, dramatically. Some of them below random chance on binary, binary questions. and then we, we clustered the failures and found, I think nine, systematic patterns, like orientation and direction, counting, state, presence of specific features, viewpoint, and so on.

So to your, to your question of, of how much of this is vision versus language. I, I would say the, the majority of it, is, is the vision side, and, and, and here's, here's my reasoning. If the, if the information is simply not in the tokens, the language model has, has no way to recover it. It's a, it's an information bottleneck in the very literal sense, right? the, the LLM can be as smart as you want, but if the, the encoder collapsed two different images into, into nearly the same vector, then, then downstream there's, there's nothing you can do. and, and that connects to what I said earlier, that we, we don't have a mechanism to let the model go back and, and look at the image again. It's a, it's a one-shot, lossy compression.

but, but I want to be careful here, because I, I don't think it's the vision architecture that's, that's at fault. It's, it's really the supervision. CLIP is trained on, on alt-text, and the alt-text almost never says which direction the dog is facing. so the, the contrastive objective has, has zero incentive to preserve that information. it's not that convolution or, or ViT cannot represent orientation, it's that nothing in the training signal asked it to. and, and that's why DINOv2 does keep it, because self-supervised objectives, they, they have to reconstruct or, or match at, at a much finer granularity. So again it, it kind of comes back to, to data and, and what you train the model on, rather than, the, the architecture.

and, and the language side is, is not innocent either, I would say. The, the models are, are very confident when they, when they get it wrong, and, part of that is the, the instruction tuning data, which is, mostly captions and, and conversations that, that don't require you to look carefully. so you, you learn to, to produce a plausible-sounding answer from the, the language prior. but I, I think that's, that's secondary.

and, and the, the fix we, we tried in that paper was, was pretty simple, just, mixture of features, mixing DINOv2 features with CLIP features. We tried, additive and interleaved, and, and the interleaved one, works, reasonably well, it, it improves the visual grounding without, without hurting instruction following too much. but I, I would say it's, it's a patch, not, not a real solution. The, the real solution is, is better vision, representation learning with, with supervision that actually, demands these details. Yeah.

r001.rationale: The response explains that CLIP is trained on image alt-text that usually captures broad semantic content, not details such as which direction an object faces, so it has little incentive to preserve spatial relations.

r002.rationale: It states that the remedy is representation learning with supervision that explicitly demands fine-grained visual details, including spatial distinctions such as orientation and direction.

grok.text:
Yeah. Thanks. And yes, the title is from the Kubrick film. We liked it because these models sound like they can see. They describe an image very fluently, but on some very basic visual details, their eyes are kind of shut.

So MMVP stands for Multimodal Visual Patterns. That’s the benchmark we introduced in that paper.

The motivation was pretty simple. We were looking at multimodal LLMs, LLaVA-style models, models that take a CLIP-like vision encoder, map those features into the language model, and then answer questions about the image. And they fail on surprisingly simple visual questions. Things a person would never get wrong. Which way something is facing. Whether a small object is there or not. Counting. Color of a particular part. Spatial relations. Not the hard reasoning questions. Just, did you actually see this.

And we wanted to know where that failure comes from. Is it the language model? Is it the alignment, the projector between vision and language? Or is it the vision encoder itself?

So we looked at CLIP, which at the time was the default vision encoder for almost all of these systems. And we constructed what we call CLIP-blind pairs. Pairs of images that to a human are clearly different, but CLIP’s embedding thinks they are very similar. High cosine similarity. CLIP cannot tell them apart. From those pairs we extracted visual patterns that CLIP systematically misses, and then we built MMVP as questions around those patterns.

What we found is that models using CLIP-like encoders fail on these questions in a very correlated way. Even strong models. The language model can be extremely capable, but if the visual information was never in the embedding, it cannot recover it. There is no looking back at the pixels. Everything is already encoded into a fixed set of vision tokens.

So to your question, how much of this bottleneck is a vision problem versus a language-model problem versus an alignment problem. For this particular failure mode, I would say a large part is really a vision-encoder problem. That’s the main message of the paper. Alignment can lose some information too, and language models have strong priors, so they sometimes answer from language instead of from the image. That’s real. But the CLIP-blind pairs are a pretty clean demonstration that if two images are collapsed already in the vision embedding, downstream, no amount of language modeling is going to separate them.

This is also what I was saying earlier. In the current framework, the image is encoded once, and then the rest of the model never really goes back to the image. So whatever the vision encoder drops is gone. Mixing different vision encoders, CLIP plus something more spatially aware, can help a bit. Higher resolution, letting the model look back at the image, putting vision more natively into the language model, I think those are the directions that actually address this, rather than just scaling the language model further.

gemini.text:
Yeah. So MMVP stands for Multimodal Visual Patterns. 

And to summarize the paper, the starting point was this observation about CLIP. As we know, almost all popular multimodal LLMs, like LLaVA and many others, use a pre-trained CLIP vision encoder to encode images into visual tokens, which are then fed into the language model. But what we found is that CLIP has systematic blind spots. We identified what we call "CLIP-blind pairs"—these are pairs of images that are clearly very different to human eyes, like having different spatial orientations, different counts of objects, or different patterns, but when you feed them into CLIP, their embedding vectors have extremely high cosine similarity. To CLIP, they look essentially identical.

And because the multimodal LLM relies on this vision encoder, when you give it these images and ask basic visual questions, the model completely fails or hallucinates. It's like the model's "eyes" are shut, hence the title. So we collected these systematic failure cases into the MMVP benchmark to evaluate how multimodal models handle these visual patterns.

Now, to your question about how much of this bottleneck is a vision problem versus a language or alignment problem: I strongly believe this is fundamentally a vision problem—specifically, a visual encoder problem. 

Because if the information is lost at the visual encoding stage, there's nothing the downstream language model can do. No matter how smart the LLM is, no matter how many billions of parameters it has, or how much instruction tuning or RLHF you do, if the visual tokens don't contain the distinction between the two images, the LLM simply cannot extract what isn't there. It's an information bottleneck.

And the reason this happens goes back to how CLIP is trained. CLIP is trained with contrastive learning on web image-text pairs. But internet text captions are very high-level and coarse. People describe "a dog playing in the park," but they don't describe the exact texture, the 3D geometry, the precise spatial relationship, or every tiny detail in the background. So to optimize the contrastive objective, CLIP learns to discard all the visual details that aren't useful for matching with text captions. It acts like a very aggressive, lossy compression of the visual world.

So I think that's a big lesson: we cannot just treat the vision encoder as a solved, off-the-shelf component. If we want multimodal LLMs to achieve genuine visual understanding, we really need to rethink the visual representations—whether by integrating self-supervised vision models like DINO, using multi-scale features, or scaling up visual pre-training with richer signals. Until we fix the visual encoder, multimodal models are always going to suffer from this visual blindness.

r001.rationale: The response explains that CLIP’s coarse image-caption contrastive training emphasizes high-level semantics and discards details such as precise spatial relationships, causing failures on spatial-relational distinctions.

r002.rationale: The response suggests richer visual training signals and alternative representations, but does not clearly state that models must be trained on spatial-relational tasks or objectives.

kimi.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, thanks for the question. So MMVP stands for Multimodal Visual Patterns, it, it's the benchmark we built for this, for this project. So the, the basic question we want to investigate is, when these multimodal LLMs fail on seemingly very simple visual questions, like, like which direction is the object facing, or, or how many of, of a particular thing are there, where is the failure really coming from? And the surprising fact we found is that there exist, what we call CLIP-blind pairs, which are pairs of images that are clearly, clearly different to humans, but the, the CLIP vision encoder maps them into almost identical embeddings. And we found a very strong correlation, that for the questions that differ only in these, in these CLIP-blind aspects, the models, like GPT-4V and the open source models, they fail, systematically. So we divided these patterns into, I believe nine categories, like orientation and direction, counting, positional relations, color, reading texts, viewpoints, and so on, and, and built MMVP from that.

And to answer your question, I, I do think a large portion of it is, is really a vision problem. Because it's, it's kind of what I, I mentioned earlier, if the information is already lost at the encoding stage, the, the language model can do nothing about it, right? It's, it's garbage in, garbage out. So people, people tend to attribute these failures to reasoning or alignment, but our study shows the vision encoder is a, a surprisingly big bottleneck. That being said, I'm, I'm not saying alignment and language don't matter. There are definitely failures from, from the fusion side, like the resolution you feed the images at, how the vision tokens are, are interfaced, and some are genuine, reasoning failures. But, and, and we also proposed a simple fix, we call it Mixture of Features, which is to, to interleave the CLIP features with, self-supervised features like DINOv2, which are, which are trained without language and are better at, pure visual grounding. And that alone fixes a lot of these failures. Yeah.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, yeah, thank you. So, so the title, yes, it's from the movie. so Shengbang Tong, who was a student with us at NYU at that time, he, he led this work. so MMVP stands for Multimodal Visual Patterns. It's, it's a benchmark. And the, the idea of the paper is, is really simple. so back then, people were surprised by these, multimodal LLMs, like GPT-4V, LLaVA, but at the same time, they, they fail on some very, very simple visual questions, like, is the dog facing left or right? Is, is the, the window open or closed? how many, how many legs does this animal have? Very, very basic things that, that a child could answer. And, we wanted to know why.

So our, our hypothesis was that the problem is in the vision encoder, because almost all of these models at that time used CLIP as the vision encoder, and CLIP is, is trained with language contrastive, contrastive to language. So, so it only learns what, what the caption tells it to learn. And the, the way we, we tested this is, we, we find what we call CLIP-blind pairs. So we, we take two images that CLIP thinks are almost the same, like the cosine similarity in CLIP space is very, very high, but in, in a vision-only model, like DINOv2, a self-supervised model, they, they look very different. So, so the two images are, are clearly different to, to a human, but CLIP cannot tell them apart. And then we ask humans to, to write a question about the difference between these two images, and, and that's, that's MMVP.

And it turns out, all the models, including GPT-4V at that time, they, they perform very poorly. some of them, some of them are below random guessing, because they, they answer the same thing for both images. And the, the important part is, when we scale CLIP, like larger model, more data, higher resolution, most of these, we, we summarize like nine visual patterns, orientation, counting, color, viewpoint, this kind of stuff, most of them do not improve with scale. So, so scaling the language contrastive objective is, is not fixing it.

So to, to your question, whether it's a vision problem or a language problem, my, my answer would be, it's, it's mostly a vision problem, at least in this, in this setting. Because, the CLIP-blind pairs are found without any language model, right? It's, it's just the, the encoder itself cannot see the difference. And, and if the encoder cannot see it, the, the LLM can, can do nothing about it. This goes back to what I said earlier, there's no mechanism to look back at the image. Everything is already compressed into the tokens. and, and when the model doesn't see the, the information, it, it falls back on the language prior. So you, you could say the hallucination is a language model behavior, but the root cause is that the visual information never, never got in. And, and we, we also showed a simple fix. We call it mixture of features. If you interleave DINOv2 features with CLIP features, the, the grounding gets noticeably better, and the, the instruction following is, is not really hurt.

But, but I, I want to be careful. I, I wouldn't say it's, it's only vision. Alignment also matters, because even with a good encoder, the, the connector between the vision and language, the projector, is trained with, with very little data compared to the, the language model. So the, the language model can still, kind of override the vision. but, but I think the, the first order problem is that we have been treating the, the vision encoder as, as solved, like just take CLIP and, and move on. And, and it's, it's, it's clearly not solved. so I think the, the vision side deserves much more, much more attention than what, what it got, at least back then. Yeah.
